messages.text: I'm a full-time college student at MTSU and broke. Can I get food stamps?

Maybe. College students have extra rules for food assistance (SNAP, once called food stamps), but many can still get it.

**What I found**
- Tennessee's rules say a student enrolled at least half time must meet one extra condition. Examples are working about 20 hours a week (80 hours a month), being in a work-study program, or caring for a young child. This is from search summaries of the state's student policy, Tennessee DHS Policy 24.27. I couldn't open the official pages myself, so please treat it as a first look. Other exemptions may apply, such as getting a disability benefit or being a single parent of a child under 12.
- If you live on campus and a meal plan covers more than half your meals, you generally can't get SNAP.
- A student who meets one of these conditions still has to meet the regular income limits.

I'm not going to say whether you might qualify yet. I need a few details, and I'll then check the current income limits.

1. Do you have a job or a work-study award? If you have a job, about how many hours a week do you work?
2. Do you live on campus with a meal plan, and do you have any kids?

Once I know that, I'll ask a few quick questions about your household, income, and rent.

**Sources** (search results only, not pages I could open)
- [Tennessee DHS Policy 24.27, SNAP Students in Higher Education](https://TN.gov/content/dam/tn/human-services/documents/Policy%2024.27%20SNAP%20Students%20in%20Higher%20Educ.pdf)
- [Mass Legal Services: SNAP rules for college students](https://www.masslegalservices.org/food4students)

Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services (DHS) decides who gets SNAP. You can still apply even if it looks unlikely. For free local help, call 211.
yeah I have a job, about 10 hours a week. no work-study. I live in an apartment off campus, not in the dorms, and I don't have a meal plan. no kids.

Thanks. With about 10 hours a week and no work-study, SNAP looks **unlikely** for now. The usual work condition for half-time or full-time students is about 20 hours a week (80 hours a month). You can still apply, and only Tennessee DHS decides.

A few other things can also count as a student exemption. Do any of these fit you?
- You have a disability, or you get disability benefits (like SSI).
- You get Families First (TANF) cash help.
- You're in a job-training program run through the state.
- You're under 18, or 50 or older.

Also, is there any chance of picking up more hours? Averaging 80 hours a month (about 18.5 a week) would meet the work condition. Your hours might also vary week to week, so tell me if they do.

If none of these fit, I can still help with other options. For example, some students may qualify for TennCare (health coverage) or find campus food pantries. If you want, I can look up MTSU's pantry and what else is available.

Source: [Tennessee DHS Policy 24.27, SNAP Students in Higher Education](https://TN.gov/content/dam/tn/human-services/documents/Policy%2024.27%20SNAP%20Students%20in%20Higher%20Educ.pdf). I only saw this through search results because the file wouldn't open for me. For free local help, call 211.

Search results describe the core rules, but none of them is the USDA's own page, so treat these as secondary summaries and check the USDA guidance directly.

- **Half-time threshold:** Enrollment below half-time generally avoids the student rules. Students enrolled less than half-time need only meet the standard SNAP income and eligibility rules, with no special student criteria. Half-time is set by each school. The institution of higher education determines what counts as half-time enrollment.

- **Work-hours exemption:** Students at half-time or more typically need one exemption. Working 20 hours is the main one. Some states average hours over a month rather than applying a weekly test. Many states have received a waiver allowing them to average hours of employment over month. Louisiana's version uses an average of 20 hours per week or 80 hours per month.

- **Work-study exemption:** Participation in a federal or state work-study program qualifies. Massachusetts goes further and counts students who were awarded work study and have not refused a work study job. Other states may apply it differently, so check your state's rules.

- **Other exemptions:** The list also includes caring for a child under 6, caring for a child aged 6 to 11 when no child care is available, certain single parents, disability, on-the-job training, TANF, and being under 18 or 50 or older. Students who meet an exemption must also meet all other SNAP eligibility requirements.

- **Meal plans:** If you live on campus and your meal plan covers more than half of your meals, you are generally not eligible for SNAP.

- **Exempt from the student rules does not mean exempt from everything:** The standard income limits and general SNAP requirements still apply. Some sources say the ABAWD 3-month time limit and work rules do not apply to students who qualify as an eligible student.

Rules vary by state, and the sources above include state-specific pages (Massachusetts, Louisiana, Colorado, Pennsylvania). The USDA's "SNAP Benefits for Students" page is the authoritative federal reference, but it did not appear in these results.

The search turned up the state's official college-student guidance, plus several secondary sites of mixed quality.

**Official sources:**
- The Tennessee DHS policy 24.27 (effective May 2019) governs SNAP for students in higher education. It says a student who meets none of the student eligibility criteria is ineligible. A student who does not meet any of the student eligibility criteria is ineligible to participate in SNAP.
- A TN.gov student eligibility guide lists the qualifying conditions as yes/no questions. These include being enrolled at least half-time while working a set number of hours, participating in work-study, or caring for a young child. It also notes that students who live in dorms and receive more than half their meals from a meal plan are not eligible for SNAP benefits. Qualifying students are subject to the regular income and asset limits for SNAP eligibility.
- A TN.gov college guide lists qualifying categories including work-study, working 80 hours per month, caring for a child under 6, a single parent enrolled full-time with a child under 12, and receiving TANF or Social Security benefits.

**Secondary sources:**
- Several general guides say college students face stricter rules and generally must be enrolled at least half-time unless they meet an exemption. These are not official and some are thin, so they should be checked against DHS.
- A 2021 college flyer describes a temporary federal expansion tied to the 2020–2021 academic year and EFC of 0. That expansion was temporary, so it likely no longer applies.

**Applying:** Applications can be submitted online through the state's DHS portal or in person at a local DHS county office.

The official policy and TN.gov guides are the most reliable for current rules, and the income limits should be confirmed on the DHS website, since they change.
